passage:
It happened at the bus stop on an ordinary Tuesday. Nothing bad was going on. Suddenly my heart started pounding like a drum, the road tilted, and my hands went tingly. I thought I was dying. I grabbed Papa's sleeve. "Papa, something's wrong with me." Papa didn't panic. He sat me on the bench, held my hand and said, "I'm right here. It will pass. Breathe with me." He kept his voice slow. I watched his chest go up and down, and after a while mine copied it. The pounding faded. The road stayed still. Later the doctor checked me and said my heart was fine. I still don't know why it happened. But I remember Papa's calm voice.
Aadhya

qa.q: Where did it happen?
qa.a: At the bus stop, on an ordinary Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Aadhya believe was happening when the road tilted?
qa.a: Aadhya was terrified and thought of dying, because the heart pounded and the hands tingled for no clear reason.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped most?
qa.a: Papa stayed calm, sat Aadhya on the bench, held a hand and breathed slowly so Aadhya could copy him, and later a doctor checked Aadhya.

qa.q: What might Papa have felt when Aadhya grabbed his sleeve?
qa.a: Papa may have felt worried inside, but kept his voice slow so his calm could steady Aadhya.

grounding: A child's sudden pounding heart, dizziness and fear of dying come with no clear trigger and pass with a calm adult close by.

passage:
Sick room note, Friday. Urmila D'Souza, school nurse.
At 11:15 Nandini (Class 7) was brought in from the library by a classmate. She was gasping, both hands on her chest, saying, "My heart's going to burst. Am I going mad?" Her face was pale and her fingers trembled. Nothing upsetting had happened, she said; she had just been reading.
I kept my voice low and slow: "You're safe. I'm staying right here. This feeling is frightening, and it will pass." I didn't leave her side. We breathed together, long out-breaths. After a while her hands loosened and she asked for water.
I phoned her mother before lunch, explained what I saw and suggested a check-up with their family doctor. Nandini can come to me any time she feels it starting.

qa.q: What had Nandini been doing just before it started?
qa.a: Nandini had just been reading in the library.

qa.q: What was Nandini afraid of during the episode?
qa.a: Nandini was terrified that her heart would burst and that she was going mad.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's actions mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Urmila stayed right beside Nandini, spoke low and slow and breathed with her; that calm presence carried her until the feeling passed.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother feel after Urmila's phone call?
qa.a: Nandini's mother would likely be worried, but reassured that Nandini was cared for and that a doctor's check-up is planned.

grounding: A preteen's sudden pounding heart and fear of going mad arrive with no trigger and ease with calm adult presence, followed by a doctor's check-up.

passage: In the school library, Dhruv was reading a comic when his heart suddenly began to slam. The shelves seemed to tilt. His hands tingled. I'm dying, he thought. Or going mad. He stumbled to the librarian's desk. 'Ma'am, something's wrong with me!' Arohi Ma'am came round the desk at once and sat him on a low chair. She didn't rush or panic. 'I'm right here, Dhruv. You're safe. Let's breathe together, slowly.' She breathed with him, in and long out, her hand resting on his shoulder. She sent a student to fetch the school nurse. Slowly, over some minutes, the pounding eased. Dhruv shook and cried a little. 'I thought I was dying.' 'That sounded very frightening,' she said. The nurse checked him and phoned his parents, who took him to the doctor that evening to be sure.

qa.q: What was Dhruv reading when his heart began to slam?
qa.a: A comic.

qa.q: What was Dhruv thinking when the shelves seemed to tilt?
qa.a: He was terrified, thinking he was dying or going mad.

qa.q: What did Arohi Ma'am do that mattered most?
qa.a: She stayed calm, stayed with him and breathed slowly with him while someone fetched the nurse.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's parents feel when the nurse phoned?
qa.a: They were probably alarmed and worried, and wanted a doctor to check him that evening.

grounding: Shows a child's sudden pounding heart, dizziness and fear of dying with no clear trigger, the sensations passing, and a calm adult staying close.

passage:
Friday: Tushar, twelve, was watching cricket with his father Kamal when his heart began to race for no reason. His vision went fuzzy. 'Papa, I'm going crazy!' Kamal switched off the TV and held his hand. 'I'm here. Breathe with me.' After a few minutes it passed.
Monday: The doctor listened to Tushar's heart and checked him carefully. 'Your body is healthy. What happened is scary, but it passes. Tell an adult if it comes again.'
The following Sunday: On the bus to his uncle's, the racing started again, smaller. Tushar gripped the seat and remembered: it passes. He told Kamal, 'It's happening.' Kamal nodded calmly and breathed with him. This time, Tushar watched out of the window until it faded.

qa.q: What were Tushar and Kamal watching when it first happened?
qa.a: Cricket.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel on the Sunday bus compared to Friday?
qa.a: He was still frightened but steadier, because he remembered it passes and told Kamal straight away.

qa.q: Which of Kamal's responses helped most?
qa.a: Staying calm, holding Tushar's hand and breathing with him each time.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt on the first Friday?
qa.a: Kamal was probably shocked and worried, but kept calm on the outside for Tushar.

grounding: Shows a preteen's sudden racing heart and fear of going crazy with no clear trigger, the sensations passing, and a calm adult's presence mattering most.

passage: Aadhya, come, sit. You think your Sarita Nani was never scared? When I was ten, in our village, I was sitting in the temple courtyard shelling peanuts. Nothing was wrong. Then suddenly my heart went thud-thud-thud like a drum at a wedding, the courtyard spun, and I was sure I was going to die right there among the peanut shells. I screamed for my Amma. She came running from the well with the pot still on her hip. She didn't shout or cry. She put the pot down, took me in her lap and hummed the song she used for the goats. 'It will pass, it will pass.' And it did. Later my father took me to the doctor in town, who said my heart was strong. Many years later I understood what it was.

qa.q: What was young Sarita doing in the temple courtyard?
qa.a: Shelling peanuts.

qa.q: What was young Sarita feeling when the courtyard spun?
qa.a: She was terrified, sure that she was going to die.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Sarita in the courtyard?
qa.a: Her Amma put the pot down, took her in her lap and hummed calmly until the fear passed.

qa.q: How might Sarita's Amma have felt, running from the well?
qa.a: She was probably frightened for her daughter but chose to stay calm and steady for her.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a child's sudden pounding heart and fear of dying with no trigger, and how a calm adult presence helped it pass.

passage: Ten minutes before the annual day show, the power went out backstage. In the pitch dark, Tenzin's heart suddenly began pounding so hard it hurt. The room tilted, both hands tingled, and a terrible thought grabbed hold: I'm dying. Tenzin gasped and grabbed the curtain. Jaya Ma'am found Tenzin by torchlight, sat down on the floor right there and said slowly, 'I'm here. You're safe. Breathe out with me, long and slow.' She didn't rush or ask questions, just kept her voice low and steady. After some minutes the wave passed, leaving Tenzin shaky and tearful. Jaya Ma'am phoned Tenzin's parents that evening and suggested a check-up with the doctor, just to be sure.

qa.q: What did Tenzin grab in the dark?
qa.a: The curtain.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel during the episode?
qa.a: Tenzin felt terrified, with a pounding heart, dizziness and a sudden fear of dying.

qa.q: What did Jaya Ma'am do that mattered most?
qa.a: She stayed calmly present, sitting close, speaking slowly and breathing with Tenzin, then phoned the parents and suggested a doctor's check.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's parents have felt after the call?
qa.a: They probably felt worried but reassured that Jaya Ma'am had stayed with Tenzin and suggested a check-up.

grounding: A preteen's first panic-like episode feels terrifying, and a calm adult's presence matters most until it passes.
